title: MEP-CMAP Analyser
description:
MEP-CMAP Analyser is a BIDS-compliant, open-source, cross-platform desktop application for processing, quantifying and group-analysing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and electromyography (EMG) neurophysiology recordings. It is built for researchers who need reproducible, auditable waveform analysis without writing custom scripts for every study.

The tool is not limited to a single measure or paradigm. It handles motor evoked potentials (MEPs), compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs), cortical silent periods (cSPs), M-wave recruitment curves, paired-pulse protocols such as short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF), and any other time-locked EMG response measurable by peak-to-peak amplitude, onset latency or area under the curve. It operates on continuous recordings, pre-epoched trial stacks, and EMG bursts recorded without stimulation.

Capabilities

  • Direct import of Spike2, LabChart, EDF/BDF, AcqKnowledge and generic delimited text files, with a guided one-time wizard for arbitrary tabular layouts
  • Configurable filtering, including band-pass, notch and harmonic suppression, with live preview
  • Automated detection of response onset, offset and duration, peak-to-peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, area under the curve and cortical silent period duration, each overridable per trial
  • Eight onset detection methods spanning derivative, derivative-ratio, amplitude-threshold, energy-operator and change-point approaches, with an optional median across them and per-trial reporting of how far they disagree
  • Automated outlier screening with an interactive review step, so exclusion decisions are explicit, persistent and recorded in the output
  • An interactive per-trial data inspector for marker adjustment, annotation and exclusion
  • Mmax normalisation with robust plateau detection across full recruitment curves, supramaximal clusters or a single M-wave
  • Compensation of evoked-potential magnitude for pre-stimulus spinal motoneurone excitability by quantile regression, following the method of Carson (2026, Journal of Physiology 604.14, 5731-5757), verified against the author's published reference implementation
  • Paired-pulse ratio computation with multiple reference assignments per file
  • Trial-level and summary CSV output, a group-level file formatted for linear mixed-effects modelling, per-trial waveform bundles, and BIDS-style derivatives with provenance

Changes in version 1.4.0

  • The licence changes to the GNU General Public License version 3. Versions 1.3.3 and earlier were released under the MIT Licence and remain so; that grant cannot be withdrawn, and anyone who obtained those releases keeps the rights they were given. From this version the project is GPL-3, which was necessary in order to incorporate work derived from the TMS Analysis ToolBox (Cunningham, Zhang and Cahn, 2021), a GPL-3 project whose terms require derivative works to carry the same licence. The practical consequence is that software which incorporates this one must also be distributed under GPL-3; use of the application to analyse data, and publication of results obtained with it, are unaffected.
  • The epoch window is now set per stimulus type. The interval cut around each stimulus, and shown in the data inspector, is a property of the response rather than of the recording: a cortical silent period requires several hundred milliseconds after the pulse, an M-wave a few tens, and one shared window meant truncating the first or carrying an order of magnitude of unnecessary samples through every trial of the second. Pre- and post-stimulus extents appear as columns on the labels tab, seeded from a preference and following it while left unedited. The former file-wide fields have been removed from the feature detection tab, where neither was display-only despite being labelled so and one additionally set the inspector's zoom; what remains there is the baseline given to the detectors, which genuinely is one setting for the recording. A file whose stimulus types share a window behaves exactly as before. Windows are shortened to fit a pre-epoched recording, and the shortening is reported rather than applied silently, because a window reaching past the stored epoch draws its baseline from the previous trial's response.
  • Preview detection. Detection settings can be tried on chosen trials before committing to a run. The preview reads its settings from the same snapshot the analysis takes, cuts trials with the same epoching and event delay, and opens the ordinary data inspector read-only, so markers are drawn where the detector places them but cannot be dragged and nothing is written. Trials are chosen from a list defaulting to an even spread across the session rather than the first few, the opening trials being where a participant is freshest and least informative about whether a setting is right. Two things a preview cannot reproduce are stated rather than hidden: amplitude window anchoring is computed from a completed run, and outlier decisions do not exist yet.
  • Configured event sources now reach the analysis. Sources were previously read only to populate the labels tab, so a configured threshold changed what was displayed while the analysis went on reading the file's own markers by name. They are held per channel, since a trigger that is clean on one electrode can sit near the noise floor on another and a bilateral protocol has a separate stimulator per limb, and they are recorded in the derivative sidecar so a run states how its stimuli were identified. The dialogue that configures them now previews every kind of source, with a whole-recording view and a single-event view that can be stepped through or jumped to by number.
  • CED Signal MATLAB exports are read. Frames are treated as pre-epoched trials, with the frame state becoming the stimulus type and the stored epoch reported so analysis windows are clamped to it. These files are written in MATLAB version 7.3, which the older MATLAB readers cannot open, so h5py is now a dependency and is bundled into the pre-built binaries. The reader was written from the files themselves rather than from any other toolbox's source.
  • Every setting on the labels and feature detection tabs carries its own explanation, shown by hovering over the marker beside it or clicking to keep it open. The prose that previously stood above those tables described a handful of settings each while occupying the vertical space the tables needed, and sat far enough from the fields that reading it meant holding a column name in mind. Where a setting's meaning depends on the state of another, the explanation follows that state.
  • Several channels may now be analysed from one recording. The analysis runs once per selected channel, in sequence, and each pass uses that channel's own configuration: labels, blanking gaps, event delays, silent period assignment, normalisation references and latency profiles. An ipsilateral silent period recorded on one channel and a contralateral motor evoked potential on another are different muscles responding to the same marker, and they require different latency windows; a single shared table could not express that. Channels are chosen when a Spike2 recording is first opened, in a dialogue that now offers a tick list rather than a single choice, or afterwards from a control beside the channel selector. No channel is designated primary, since every selected channel is analysed identically and a primary would imply a hierarchy that does not exist; the first selected is simply where configuration begins. The confirmation button steps through the selected channels in turn and the analysis will not start while any remain unconfirmed, so a channel cannot be selected and then forgotten. A channel not yet configured begins from defaults rather than inheriting the previous channel's table, because inheriting one silently is a way to apply another muscle's latency window without noticing. Where more than one channel is analysed the output filenames carry a channel entity so that the passes do not overwrite one another, and a channel column is written to the trial and summary files in every case, so that a single-channel result can still join a multi-channel dataset. The analysis pipeline itself is unchanged: it receives one channel's settings per run and knows nothing of the others.
  • Where stimulus events come from is now stated explicitly. Every reader exposed the same function for retrieving stimulation times, and every reader meant something different by its one argument: the event channel to read, the label to attach to threshold detections, or nothing at all. The shared signature was a coincidence of naming rather than an interface, so asking a reader for something it did not already do was impossible, the one parameter that could have carried the request having already been given another meaning. LabChart MATLAB files consequently yielded their comment table and nothing else, which was not so much a missing feature as a missing question: the format carries comments, digital inputs and fixed-interval sampling, and only the first could be asked for. Events are now drawn from an explicit list of sources of three kinds: the events the file already carries, whether comments, markers, annotations or event channels; a crossing on any analogue channel, specified by level, edge and a refractory period so that a pulse which rings is counted once; and fixed timing, for recordings triggered by something the file does not record. Several may be combined, each contributing its own stimulus type. Threshold and interval detection depend on nothing but a waveform and a time base, both of which every reader already provides, so they are implemented once and available to all of them; a reader need only declare which of its channels are analogue. The previous function is unchanged and is what a source of the first kind calls, so a file configured as every file was configured before passes through no new code, a contract verified against real recordings in six formats and against files the tests construct themselves in three more.
  • Two sources producing the same stimulus type is reported as an error; two producing events at nearly the same instant are kept and reported. Combining the former would give a trial count matching neither source, and a disagreement of that kind is far more likely to be a misconfiguration than an intention. The latter cannot be resolved from the data at all: a comment written by software immediately after a trigger pulse is indistinguishable from two genuine stimuli a few milliseconds apart, and merging them would silently halve the trial count of a paired-pulse protocol. Both circumstances are described in the log rather than absorbed.
  • A preview for choosing a threshold level. A level cannot be verified by reading it: two volts is correct or incorrect depending on the trigger's amplitude, its baseline and whether the pulse rings, none of which is apparent from the field in which it was typed. The chosen channel is now drawn with the level across it, every detected crossing marked, and a count that changes as the level does. The trace is reduced for display by taking the minimum and maximum of each displayed column rather than by subsampling: a stimulus trigger is a single-sample transient, and on a two-thousand-second recording sampled at five kilohertz, subsampling produced a flat line while the detector found two hundred events. A preview which conceals the pulses is worse than none, the level then being set against a trace showing nothing of what the detector responds to.
  • Several channels may be selected when a file is opened, and the assignment is shown every time. The channel assignment dialogue offered a single channel and appeared only when no saved assignment existed, so after the first opening the channel and trigger choices became invisible and unalterable; the only recourse was deleting the derivatives folder and the companion files by hand. These two decisions determine what the entire analysis measures. The dialogue now offers a list of tick boxes, appears whenever a file is opened with the previous choices already selected, and can be reset explicitly from the File menu. No channel is designated primary, every selected channel being analysed identically; the first selected is simply where configuration begins. Both of the tool's channel dialogues were changed, since multi-channel analysis is not a property of one file format and leaving the second as a single choice would have made the capability reachable in one format of ten.
  • Files no reader can open are identified rather than misattributed. Format detection concluded by assuming that anything unrecognised was a Spike2 text export, so a word-processor document, a configuration file or an ADInstruments native recording each failed at some later point with a message naming the wrong format. A binary file matching no known signature is now reported as unreadable, and where the extension is recognised the message states what to do instead.
  • Marker edits no longer cross between channels. A marker position is an index into one channel's waveform and means nothing when applied to another. In an analysis of several channels the second inherited the first's, which produced negative peak-to-peak amplitudes wherever the stored maximum sample fell below the stored minimum, and reported every offset as manually placed when none had been. Edits are now held separately per channel through the analysis, the interactive inspector and the session file. A session written before this change carries a single unattributed set; it is used for review of one channel, where it unambiguously belongs to the channel displayed, and disregarded in an analysis of several rather than assigned by guesswork. A negative peak-to-peak amplitude can no longer be written in any case: it is a magnitude, and the value had been propagating into the normalisation and standard-score columns as though it were meaningful.
  • A session saved by hand is now as complete as one saved automatically. The two were assembled separately and had diverged: the manual path recorded thirteen fewer settings, among them the latency profiles, both muscle-group selections, the onset detection method and every one of its parameters. Reloading such a session restored the file and most of its settings while silently reverting those, so a subsequent analysis could proceed with a latency window and a detector the analyst had not chosen, and nothing indicated it. Both paths now build the same payload. Analyses whose sessions were saved through the File menu should be checked.
  • A correction for event markers that do not coincide with the stimulus. The marker recorded in a file is not always the instant the stimulus fired: a trigger written by software after the pulse, a delay setting on the stimulator, or a different signal path for one block will each shift it, usually by a fixed amount. The consequence is not a visibly wrong latency but an epoch whose zero is wrong, so that part of the response falls into the pre-stimulus window and every measure defined relative to the baseline then fails, each in a manner resembling a separate fault. On one recording whose markers for a single condition were two milliseconds late, the derivative-ratio detector returned no onsets at all from fifteen trials, peak-to-peak amplitude was read from a shoulder rather than the peak, and the offset was reported part-way down a deflection; these were investigated as three unrelated problems before the common cause was identified. A per-stimulus-type delay is now applied when epoching, so that everything measured from zero moves with it, including reported latencies. The delay may be measured automatically from the stimulus artefact. The artefact is located by peak slope rather than peak amplitude, since it is the steepest feature in the epoch but not always the largest and an amplitude search returns the response instead on a supramaximal compound muscle action potential. Two conditions govern whether a delay is proposed at all. The first is the spread across trials: a genuine fixed delay measures a fraction of a millisecond in standard deviation, whereas markers that truly jitter measured 3.9 milliseconds on a real recording, and above a threshold the scan reports the spread and proposes nothing, a single correction being wrong on every trial rather than right on average in that case. The second is the width of the transient: where there is no artefact, the steepest feature is the response's own rising edge, which is consistent enough across trials to pass the spread test and would therefore be proposed with confidence, so a width limit distinguishes them — across two recordings the artefact measured 0.4 to 0.6 milliseconds wide at half its maximum against 4.6 milliseconds for a response edge. Nothing is applied silently: proposed values populate the interface for review, the value and whether it was measured or entered by hand are written to the sidecar, and altering a delay marks affected files as requiring reprocessing.
  • Three faults corrected in offset detection. First, the refinement stage reported its own search boundary. It scanned a fixed neighbourhood for the first sustained quiet interval, and where the fine envelope was already quiet at the start of that neighbourhood, which is the ordinary case because a centred coarse window places the crossing late, it returned the neighbourhood's lower bound. The reported offset was therefore the coarse crossing minus the envelope window on every trial: a function of a smoothing setting rather than of the signal. The refinement now walks back to the last sample that remained elevated, which removes the dependence on the search radius entirely; across envelope windows of three, five and eight milliseconds the offset now varies by six tenths of a millisecond where previously it moved with the setting. Second, the envelope baseline is now estimated by the median and median absolute deviation rather than the mean and standard deviation. The envelope is computed with a centred window, so a stimulus artefact smears backwards by half of it; the guard applied by the caller covers an artefact at zero, but one landing even slightly earlier reaches past it and a handful of contaminated samples then dominate the estimate. On a real recording this raised the return threshold seventy-three-fold relative to a neighbouring condition, and the offset was reported while the response was still at a quarter of its peak amplitude. Third, the peak-fraction floor beneath the return threshold is now disabled by default. It had been introduced to address a case in which offset detection failed on eighty of eighty-one trials, but the cause there was a sixty-millisecond duration ceiling, and once that was raised the baseline threshold alone detected every trial. What the floor does is shorten the reported offset, in proportion to the size of the response, so that it truncates most severely on the largest and cleanest responses; measured against an independent settling criterion on a real recording it shortened the offset by between forty-five and ninety-seven milliseconds depending on its value, whereas at zero the same criterion gave errors of minus 5.9 and plus 2.3 milliseconds. On a resting recording, where responses are an order of magnitude smaller, the two settings are indistinguishable.
  • The return threshold now accounts for where the signal settles. It had been derived from the pre-stimulus baseline alone, which assumes the signal returns to where it began. Measured across every condition of one session, the envelope floor late in the epoch stood between 1.3 and 2.0 times the pre-stimulus floor, so that the pre-stimulus level was a target the signal never reached and the offset was reported wherever the envelope happened to dip. The threshold is now the larger of the two. Across eight conditions of two recordings the median offset moved earlier in every case; trial-to-trial scatter improved in five and worsened in two.
  • Amplitude window anchoring falls back to the stimulus type's own latency profile. Where a stimulus type has too few detected onsets to anchor its measurement window, the fallback had been the file-wide window, which is the very setting that anchoring exists to replace and is typically placed after the peak of a compound muscle action potential. The condition already in difficulty was therefore also the one whose amplitude was truncated, while its neighbours measured correctly. On a real recording the first phase of a 3.8 millivolt response fell outside the window entirely and peak-to-peak amplitude was read from a 2.1 millivolt shoulder.
  • Data Inspector. The offset and the response duration are reported alongside the existing measures and update as markers are moved. Where a cortical silent period is detected, its start marker is the offset marker, the two being one physical event; two draggable markers for a single event may be moved apart, and the file would then record two answers to the same question. The integration window for area under the curve is tied to the onset and the offset in both directions and is reconciled whenever a trial is displayed rather than only when a marker is moved; it had previously ended at a fixed fifty milliseconds after onset and could therefore disagree with the results file. A background silent-period search that set this window for every stimulus type, including resting recordings where the concept does not apply, no longer runs for types not assigned to silent period measurement. The amplitude measurement window is now taken from the analysis rather than re-derived from the file-wide setting, so that review and analysis measure the same interval when anchoring is enabled. A failed onset detection is reported as such: the marker had fallen back to the stimulus, which read as a latency of zero, and that index was returned on saving as a manual override, silently converting a blank latency into a measured one. An option displays the stimulus type's median waveform behind the trial, this being the same waveform the derivative-ratio detector compares each trial against.
  • Selecting a range of data now describes what the selection contains. The dialogue reported the selected intervals in seconds, which says nothing about the trials within them; a recruitment curve, a block at a fixed intensity and a silent period block may occupy one recording with no visible boundary between them. The selection is now described in trials: how many of each stimulus type, and their positions in the file's own numbering, which follows the same convention as the Data Inspector. A discontinuous selection is reported as the intervals it comprises rather than collapsed to its outer bounds, since collapsing would claim more trials than were chosen.
  • Smaller changes. The sampling rate and amplitude unit are reported when a file is opened; both were read automatically but neither was shown until the analysis ran, so that opening a file gave no confirmation of what had been detected. The filter preview accepts every format the readers handle, having carried its own list of extensions that was not updated when support for EDF, BrainVision, MATLAB, AcqKnowledge and delimited text was added; a MATLAB file consequently failed to load there and the preview requested a sampling rate the file had already declared. The guidance on the setup tab now states what the blanking gap does to the background window. Quitting no longer prints interface errors caused by callbacks left queued against an interpreter being torn down. A latency window that contradicts the muscle group selected alongside it is now reported, the previous symptom of the two disagreeing being onsets accumulating at the lower bound of a profile the interface was no longer displaying.
  • New onset detection method: derivative ratio, after Boyles et al. (2026). Working backwards from the first peak of the response, each candidate sample is scored by the ratio of the mean absolute derivative ahead of it to the mean absolute derivative behind it, and the onset is the earliest sample still reaching a set fraction of the largest such ratio. Three gates follow: a latency ceiling, a requirement that most of the first few forward derivatives exceed the baseline mean derivative, and a requirement that the mean derivative over a following window exceed the baseline mean by a multiple of its standard deviation. The method is independent of every other detector in the tool in what it measures, being neither a threshold crossing, nor a run length in the derivative, nor a cumulative change point, and that independence is its principal value as a member method. Ported from the MATLAB reference implementation in the TMSMultiLab library. Off by default and not among the default member methods.
  • Detectors may now be supplied with a condition average. The derivative-ratio method requires a grand-mean waveform in order to reject trials whose peak falls far from the expected latency. The analysis supplies the outlier-screened median waveform of each stimulus type, which is the same waveform onset anchoring already used and is now computed whether or not anchoring is enabled. No other detector consults it and none changes behaviour as a consequence. The Data Inspector supplies the same waveform, so that a trial is judged against the same landmark during review as during analysis.
  • Three details of the reference implementation are corrected, each reversible. The published MATLAB code contains three behaviours that its own comments contradict. Each is corrected by default and reproduced exactly by a single option, because a correction that cannot be disabled makes the published method impossible to reproduce, while one applied silently makes a result attributable to neither version. First, the slope comparison window is fixed in samples rather than in milliseconds. The paper states the width both as five samples and, in its figure legend, as two and a half milliseconds; the two agree only at the two kilohertz used in that study. The reference implementation indexes with the literal five, so the window is five samples however the data were sampled, giving two and a half milliseconds at two kilohertz, one millisecond at five kilohertz and half a millisecond at ten kilohertz. Measured on a real recording, detection under the sample-count behaviour fell from eighteen trials in twenty at one kilohertz to eleven in twenty at five kilohertz; at exactly two kilohertz the two versions return identical results. This tool uses the published duration. Second, the amplitude gate compares the response's peak-to-peak amplitude against the baseline maximum rather than the baseline peak-to-peak amplitude, and is therefore approximately half as strict as its name and comment imply. Third, the peak-jitter gate compares the trial's largest peak against the condition average's first peak; on a biphasic response whose second phase is the larger, those two quantities differ by the peak-to-trough interval on every trial, so the tolerance is expended on a definitional mismatch rather than on jitter. The paper does not state which landmark it intends, so this third item is a clarification rather than a correction.
  • A stated limitation of the new method. Every one of its gates is expressed in absolute derivatives, so what it requires is that the response be spectrally richer than the baseline, and not merely larger. Measured at the published window, detection of a smooth synthetic response fell from nineteen trials in twenty at a baseline noise of 0.012 millivolts to none at all at 0.020 millivolts, while the same response carrying harmonic content still gave sixteen in twenty; the root-mean-square envelope detector scored twenty in twenty throughout that range. Quiet resting recordings sit well inside the working range, a real recording with a pre-stimulus root-mean-square of 0.0034 millivolts yielding seventeen to eighteen trials in twenty per condition, but a noisy baseline or aggressive low-pass filtering will disable it, and it fails by returning nothing rather than a wrong latency.
  • Renamed: the “consensus” method is now “median across methods”. The former name implied that the agreed value was the correct one, which is precisely the inference the method's own outputs caution against: detectors sharing an assumption may be wrong together, and two of the members are not independent, one taking the other's answer as its starting point. The trial-level column Onset_Consensus(ms) becomes Onset_MethodsMedian(ms), with the corresponding renaming in the method comparison tables. Sessions and preference files written by the previous release continue to work: the former method key still resolves, and the renamed preference is carried across on first load.

Note on the epoch window: analyses whose stimulus types should not share one window will differ from earlier releases, and deliberately so. A recording left at its previous settings is unchanged, since an unset per-type window falls back to the file-wide pair. Where a type is given its own window, everything measured within it follows: peak-to-peak amplitude if the window previously truncated the response, offset and duration and area under the curve if they extended beyond it. On a pre-epoched recording a window longer than the stored epoch is now shortened to fit, where a previous release would have measured the mirror-padded guard band between stitched trials and reported it as recorded signal.

Note on reproducibility: recordings analysed with an earlier release should be reprocessed if offset, duration or area under the curve was used, and any analysis whose session was saved through the File menu should be checked against the settings it was intended to use. The three corrections to offset detection change the reported offset on most recordings, and duration and area under the curve follow from it. Peak-to-peak amplitude changes only for stimulus types whose amplitude window previously fell back to the file-wide setting because too few onsets were detected. Latency changes only for stimulus types given an event delay, which is not applied unless requested. Cortical silent period and normalisation measures are unaffected. The renaming described above changes column headings but no values; a script reading Onset_Consensus(ms) by name will require updating. Recordings analysed with version 1.3.2 or earlier should be reprocessed if onset latency or area under the curve was used, for the reasons given at version 1.3.3; those analysed with version 1.3.1 or earlier for the trial-level column alignment corrected in version 1.3.2; and those analysed with the excitability compensation in version 1.2.5 or earlier for the reason noted at version 1.2.8.
